authoredPrompt: This figure carries two labeled panels, (a) and (b), each a perspective sketch of a light ray with its electric field vectors. In panel (a), a thin blue line slants from the upper left down to an arrowhead at the lower right and is annotated Direction of ray (of propagation). From one point on that line, eight bold red arrows radiate outward in the plane perpendicular to the ray, evenly spaced and pointing up, down, left, right, and along the four diagonals; four are tagged E with a vector arrow, and the group is headed Random polarization. Panel (b) repeats the same blue ray, drawn longer, with an identical red starburst near its left end. Farther along the ray sits a tan shaded ellipse labeled Polarizing filter by a curly leader and crossed by a vertical double-headed black arrow labeled Axis. Beyond the filter, a single red arrow remains on the ray, vertical and double-headed, labeled E and tied by wavy leaders to Polarization direction and Direction of ray. Setting the many-armed starburst before the filter against the lone vertical arrow after it is the comparison the two panels stage, introducing unpolarized light and the filter that passes only the field component along its own axis.
authoredInteractions:
- Slider for filter-axis angle: the learner rotates the polarizer axis, and the transmitted red E arrow stays aligned with the selected axis, showing that unpolarized light becomes polarized along the filter direction.
- Toggle between unpolarized and after-filter view: the learner switches from the many-direction starburst to the single transmitted arrow, making the contrast between random polarization and one selected polarization direction explicit.
- Click on a single incoming E direction: the selected red input arrow is isolated, its component parallel to the filter axis is highlighted through the filter while the perpendicular component fades, clarifying component selection for one chosen incident direction.
authoredContext:
The Sun and many other light sources produce waves that have the electric fields in random directions (the figure(a)). Such light is said to be unpolarized, because it is composed of many waves with all possible directions of polarization. Polaroid materials—which were invented by the founder of the Polaroid Corporation, Edwin Land—act as a polarizing slit for light, allowing only polarization in one direction to pass through. Polarizing filters are composed of long molecules aligned in one direction. If we think of the molecules as many slits, analogous to those for the oscillating ropes, we can understand why only light with a specific polarization can get through. The axis of a polarizing filter is the direction along which the filter passes the electric field of an EM wave.

The slender arrow represents a ray of unpolarized light. The bold arrows represent the direction of polarization of the individual waves composing the ray. (a) If the light is unpolarized, the arrows point in all directions. (b) A polarizing filter has a polarization axis that acts as a slit passing through electric fields parallel to its direction. The direction of polarization of an EM wave is defined to be the direction of its electric field.

Figure a shows a slender blue arrow pointing out of the page and to the right that is labeled direction of ray. Eight red arrows emanate from a point on the ray and are labeled as vectors E. These arrows are all in a plane perpendicular to the ray and are uniformly distributed around the ray. They are labeled as representing a random polarization. In figure b, a similar but longer ray is shown with the same red arrows emanating from a point near the left end of the ray. Farther to the right on the same ray is a thin rectangle with six equally spaced vertical slits. This rectangle is labeled polarizing filter. A vertical double headed arrow on its surface is labeled axis. To the right of the filter, centered on the ray, is a single blue double headed arrow oriented vertically that is labeled E and direction of polarization.

The figure shows the effect of two polarizing filters on originally unpolarized light. The first filter polarizes the light along its axis, decreasing its intensity by a factor of 2. When the axes of the first and second filters are aligned (parallel), then all of the polarized light passed by the first filter is also passed by the second filter. If the second polarizing filter is rotated, only the component of the light parallel to the second filter’s axis is passed. When the axes are perpendicular, no light is passed by the second filter.
sourceQmd: OpenStax University Physics, chapter 34: The Nature of Light

discrepancies: E-vector labels render as 'E□' — the combining arrow glyph (E⃗) fails to display, so the key E annotations are broken
The transmitted E arrow after the filter is double-headed, while the source shows a single upward red E arrow
Source is a flat front-on 2D diagram, but the generated figure uses an off-axis 3D view, making the starburst and filter disc tilted rather than face-on
Labels 'Direction of ray (of propagation)' and 'Polarization direction' overlap/collide near the bottom center in the rendered view
In mode (b) the source still shows the incident starburst to the left of the filter; it is present but small and crowded near the disc, weakening the two-stage composition
evaluation.notes: Correct polarization concept with excellent, pedagogically strong interactions (mode toggle, axis slider, component decomposition), but broken E-arrow glyphs, off-axis 3D camera on a flat 2D source, and label collisions hurt fidelity.
action_items: Fix the E-vector labels: use a font-safe rendering such as 'E→' via an SVG/vector arrow or plain 'E' with an arrow drawn, instead of the unsupported combining glyph that shows as a box
Use a front-on orthographic view (axis_screen_angles: null) so the starburst is viewed face-on like the source figure
Make the transmitted arrow single-headed to match the source, and separate the 'Direction of ray' and 'Polarization direction' labels so they do not overlap
